text: Old church windows are not thicker at the bottom because glass flows. Medieval panes were uneven when made, and calculations show visible sagging at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe.
In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, an organic compound, from inorganic ammonium cyanate. Textbooks say this killed vitalism overnight, but historians find the idea faded gradually over decades.
When gallium was discovered in 1875, its discoverer measured its density as 4.7 g/cm³. Mendeleev, who had predicted the element, insisted it should be about 5.9; on remeasurement, it was.
Helium was found in the Sun before it was found on Earth. Astronomers saw an unexplained yellow spectral line during the 1868 solar eclipse; William Ramsay isolated the gas on Earth only in 1895.

Whether hot water can freeze faster than cold is still disputed. Tanzanian student Erasto Mpemba reported it in 1969, but careful experiments disagree, and results depend on how "freezing" is defined.
Technetium, element 43, was the first element made artificially. In 1937 Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè found it in molybdenum foil that Ernest Lawrence had sent them from a Berkeley cyclotron.
Seaborgium, element 106, was the first element named after a living person, Glenn Seaborg; the name was approved in 1997. The only other is oganesson, for Yuri Oganessian.
Textbooks once called the noble gases inert. In 1962 Neil Bartlett let xenon meet platinum hexafluoride and got an orange-yellow solid, the first true compound of a noble gas.
Thalidomide's mirror-image forms act differently, but giving only the "safe" form would not have prevented its birth defects: the body converts each form into the other within hours.
Carvone comes in two mirror-image forms that smell different: (R)-carvone smells of spearmint and (S)-carvone of caraway seeds. Your nose can tell left from right.
In August 1897 Bayer chemist Felix Hoffmann made aspirin and, eleven days later, diacetylmorphine. Bayer trademarked the second as Heroin in 1898 and sold it as a cough suppressant.
On April 6, 1938, Roy Plunkett at DuPont opened a cylinder of tetrafluoroethylene that seemed empty but was too heavy. The gas inside had polymerized into a slippery white solid: Teflon.
Roger Sheldon's E-factor measures waste per kilogram of product. Oil refining makes under 0.1 kg of waste per kg; drug manufacturing typically makes 25 to over 100 kg.
Roughly half the world's people are fed by nitrogen fertilizer from the Haber-Bosch process, which pulls nitrogen from the air using an iron catalyst at high temperature and pressure.
"The underlying physical laws necessary for ... the whole of chemistry are thus completely known." The catch: equations "much too complicated to be soluble." (Paul Dirac, Proc. Royal Society, 1929)
The 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry went to David Baker for computational protein design and to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures from their sequences.

Relativity makes gold yellow: relativistic effects on its electrons shift its absorption into blue light, and without them it would look silvery. A 2013 calculation put mercury's melting point near 82 °C without them.

In the 1770s Benjamin Franklin poured a teaspoon of oil on a pond on Clapham Common and watched it calm about half an acre. That implies a film roughly 2 nanometers thick, though he never did the sum.
In 1989 Donald Eigler of IBM used a scanning tunneling microscope to arrange 35 xenon atoms on a chilled nickel crystal into the letters IBM, the first precise placement of single atoms.

Without its enzyme, one step in making DNA and RNA building blocks, the decarboxylation of orotidine monophosphate, has a half-life of about 78 million years. The enzyme speeds it up about 10¹⁷ times.

Rubisco, the enzyme that fixes carbon in photosynthesis, is probably the most abundant protein on Earth partly because it is so poor at its job: it handles a few CO2 molecules per second and often grabs O2 by mistake.
In 1840 Marie Lafarge was convicted of poisoning her husband after the toxicologist Mathieu Orfila used the new Marsh test, published in 1836, to find arsenic in the exhumed body.

MRI is nuclear magnetic resonance imaging. Radiologists dropped "nuclear" in the early 1980s partly so patients would not assume radiation; it refers to hydrogen nuclei, and nothing radioactive is involved.

Until 1989 many thought a single molecule could not be detected by light. That year W. E. Moerner and Lothar Kador did it with pentacene in a crystal near absolute zero, groundwork for Moerner's 2014 Nobel Prize.

Prussian blue, first made in Berlin in the early 1700s, was the first modern synthetic pigment. The same compound is now a medicine that traps radioactive cesium in the gut, used after Brazil's Goiânia accident in 1987.
A single quarry at Ytterby, near Stockholm, gave its name to four elements: yttrium, terbium, erbium and ytterbium. Minerals from it yielded several more, including holmium and thulium.
Diamond is thermodynamically unstable at Earth's surface; graphite is the more stable form of carbon. The conversion is so slow at room temperature that diamonds effectively last forever anyway.
Life uses almost only left-handed amino acids and right-handed sugars, though ordinary chemistry makes both mirror forms in equal amounts. How that one-sidedness arose is still unsolved.
"All things are poison, and nothing is without poison; only the dose makes a thing not a poison." (Paracelsus, Third Defence, 1538)
Your body holds well under a kilogram of ATP at any moment, yet it rebuilds roughly its own body weight of ATP every day, recycling each molecule hundreds of times.
